title: OpenAI Evaluation and Observability
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to design repeatable evaluations, use run observations to investigate failures, and decide whether a change improved an OpenAI-based system. After completing it, learners can connect evaluation criteria, test cases, and observed evidence instead of relying on informal impressions.
objectives: Define measurable evaluation criteria for an OpenAI-based system.
Create test cases that represent expected behavior and important failure conditions.
Use recorded inputs, outputs, outcomes, and errors to investigate evaluation failures.
Compare changes using the same test cases and criteria rather than subjective impressions.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you can write a prompt, inspect a model output, and recognize whether an output meets a stated requirement. It does not assume knowledge of a particular evaluation tool, programming language, configuration format, or statistical method.

Evaluation is the structured process of testing outputs against stated criteria. Observability, as used in this module, means retaining enough evidence from each run to understand what was tested, what happened, and why a result passed or failed.

sections.title: Define success before testing
paragraphs: Begin with the behavior the system should exhibit. Convert that behavior into criteria that can be applied consistently. A criterion should distinguish an acceptable output from an unacceptable one without depending only on a reviewer's general impression.

For example, if the requested output must contain three specific fields, the criterion should name those fields. If an answer must avoid unsupported claims, the criterion should require each factual claim to be grounded in the provided material. Clear criteria make failures easier to classify and later comparisons easier to interpret.

Use more than one test case. Include ordinary requests, difficult cases, and cases likely to expose important failures. Each test case should preserve the input, the applicable criteria, and the resulting output so that another reviewer can understand the decision.

sections.title: Observe each run
paragraphs: For every evaluated run, retain the test input, the produced output, the criteria applied, the pass or fail outcome, and any error that prevented completion. This evidence connects an evaluation result to what actually occurred.

When a test fails, inspect the evidence before changing the system. Determine whether the output violated a criterion, the test case was ambiguous, the criterion could not be applied consistently, or an error prevented a usable output. These are different failure categories and can require different responses.
Avoid treating a single successful example as proof of general improvement. A repeatable comparison uses the same relevant test cases and the same criteria before and after a change.

sections.title: Compare and iterate
paragraphs: Establish a baseline by running the current system against the selected test cases. Make one clearly identified change, run the same relevant cases again, and compare outcomes criterion by criterion.

Look for both improvements and regressions. A change can fix one failure while creating another. Preserve failed cases that represent behavior you still care about, because they can become regression tests for later changes.

If a result cannot be explained from the retained evidence, improve the observation record before drawing a conclusion. The goal is not merely to produce a score. The goal is to make decisions using repeatable tests and inspectable evidence.
sections.callout: A defensible improvement claim requires stable criteria, relevant test cases, and evidence from comparable runs.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation criterion is most consistently testable?
choices: The output should feel high quality.
The output must contain the three fields named in the request.
The output should probably satisfy most readers.
The output should be better than expected.
questions.explanation: The module explains that a criterion should distinguish acceptable from unacceptable output consistently. Naming the required fields provides a specific condition that a reviewer can check.

questions.prompt: What should you do first after an evaluated test fails?
choices: Inspect the retained input, output, criteria, outcome, and errors.
Declare that the system has regressed.
questions.explanation: The module instructs learners to inspect the retained evidence before changing the system or drawing a conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which comparison provides the strongest evidence that a change improved the system?
choices: One successful example after the change.
Different test cases and different criteria before and after the change.
The same relevant test cases and criteria before and after the change.
A reviewer's general impression of the latest output.
questions.explanation: The module states that a repeatable comparison uses the same relevant test cases and the same criteria before and after a change.

questions.prompt: Why should a failed case representing important behavior be preserved?
choices: It can serve as a regression test for later changes.
It guarantees that every future output will pass.
It removes the need to define criteria.
It proves that the original change was successful.
questions.explanation: The module says that important failed cases can become regression tests used to detect whether later changes recreate the failure.
